newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - a sweet and sour market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - a sweet and sour market.

text.p: U.S. sweet crudes should remain firm this week backed by strong refining activity and relatively thin supplies of distillate-rich crudes, traders and analysts said Monday.
However, the sour market remains under pressure from a number of directions, including the U.S. government's latest Strategic Petroleum Reserve sales and Canadian imports.
Meanwhile, outright prices, dislodged from their lofty $25-25.80 a barrel levels, will depend on gasoline stocks to keep the bull run intact, analysts said.

"We should see high levels of refining activity for the next six to 12 weeks," said John Saucer, analyst with Smith Barney in Houston, noting crude would also derive support from a "painfully narrow West Texas Intermediate/Brent arbitrage."
Over a four-week average, crude imports to the U.S. have been modest at between 7.2-7.4 million barrels per day (bpd).
This has choked off prized light/sweet crudes from the North Sea and West Africa, inspiring phenomenal rises in domestic Heavy Louisiana Sweet (HLS) and Light Louisiana Sweet.
Traders said the run-up to November pipeline scheduling last week triggered a wave of buying in typically sedate HLS, and this trend for sweets should persist into December.
"People are willing to pay over a buck in the Gulf Coast. That's very impressive," Saucer said.
He added that refiners would likely "break their backs trying to make products" because of heating oil.
The furious buying in domestic light crudes, however, was partly blamed on speculation due to non-traditional players rushing to cover shorts last minute.
But end-users were also worried about longer-term supply.
One-year term sales of LLS were seen at premiums of up to 30 cents a barrel over WTI/Cushing last week.
Traders said that hedging against price spikes signalled tighter distillate-rich crude supplies ahead, and underlined concerns that products could also run higher due to low stocks.
Venezuela's Amuay refinery cat cracker shutdown and maximization of heating oil now puts a bullish spin to gasoline, where output has been sacrificed for heating oil.
Crude oil could find itself chasing after a rising gasoline market although a bearish finish to the Nov/Dec WTI spread heralds some uncertainty for crude.
Some analysts have suggested that crude-to-gasoline and crude-to-heating oil cracks could improve a little.
Meanwhile, in contrast to the light ends, heavy sours are coming under pressure from higher exports of Canadian heavy crudes to the U.S. Midwest.
Northern tier refiners, some experiencing a loss of output due to recent problems, or with access to Canadian crudes, are flushing out West Texas Sour/Midland.
Upcoming sales of mostly light sour crudes from the U.S. government's Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), should also exert downward pressure.
